Repo: C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Windows paths, Git-Bash/PowerShell environment). Kodely, an AI website builder. No new npm dependencies allowed.

CONTEXT — read fully before writing anything:
- lib/site-records.ts, lib/site-record-render.ts, lib/site-endpoint.ts, lib/site-forms.ts — the full data foundation just built (Phase 0 + Phase 1 A-C): `SiteRecord` (projectId, kind, fields Json, status, ipHash, spam, editTokenHash, createdAt/updatedAt), same-origin-only write via `POST /__records/<kind>`, server-side-rendered read-back via `data-kodely-records="<kind>"` + `<template data-kodely-record-template>` + `{{field}}` (text-content-only interpolation, escaped), and token-based update/cancel via `GET/POST /__records/<kind>/<id>?token=...` with anti-enumeration replies. A manage-link confirmation email was just added to the create flow (read that too, it's the most recent change to site-records.ts — keep your changes additive to it, don't revert or fight it).
- app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts — where all of the above is dispatched from (GET and POST handlers for published sites), and the `SANDBOX_CSP` constant (`connect-src 'none'`, `form-action 'self'`) — this MUST NOT be relaxed by your work; everything below has to work via plain same-origin navigation/cookies, never client-side fetch.
- lib/auth.ts (Kodely's own portal login for customers signing into their Kodely dashboard) — read this ONLY to understand what NOT to reuse or share. This new work is a COMPLETELY SEPARATE trust domain: a visitor logging into a generated site at `<slug>.kodely.site` must never be confusable with, or share any session/cookie/token infrastructure with, someone logged into the Kodely portal at kodely.me. Use a distinctly-named cookie and entirely separate tables. If lib/auth.ts's cookie has no explicit `Domain` attribute (scoped to the exact host only), follow that same pattern for your new cookie — never set a `Domain` attribute that could make a cookie valid across multiple subdomains.
- lib/mail.ts and the confirmation-email code just added to site-records.ts — your pattern reference for sending a real magic-link email (same `sendMail`/`isMailConfigured`/`headerSafe`/`escapeHtml` discipline, same fire-and-forget-but-log-failures style, same non-reflective minimal content).
- prisma/schema.prisma — match existing model/index/cascade conventions exactly (look at how `SiteRecord` and `FormSubmission` relate to `Project`).
- lib/agent.ts — where the Records section you'll find there (added in the immediately prior phase) explains the write/read/manage conventions to the builder model. You'll add a parallel section for accounts.

THE GOAL: a real, working "sign in" capability for a generated site's own visitors — e.g., "log in to see your bookings" or "create an account to track your orders" — using ONLY magic-link email (passwordless). The AI must NEVER handle or generate any password/credential logic; this is precisely why magic-link, not passwords, is the only option here.

BUILD:

1. **New Prisma models**, scoped per-project (a visitor's identity on Site A is completely separate from the same email's identity on Site B — no cross-project identity linking, which keeps this simple and avoids a real privacy/correlation problem):
   - `SiteVisitor`: `id`, `projectId` (FK, cascade delete from Project), `email` (String), `createdAt`. Unique on `(projectId, email)`.
   - `SiteLoginToken`: `id`, `siteVisitorId` (FK, cascade delete), `tokenHash` (String, salted SHA-256 like every other token in this codebase — new dedicated env-var salt, same pattern as `RECORD_EDIT_TOKEN_SALT`), `expiresAt` (DateTime — 15 minutes from creation), `usedAt` (DateTime, nullable — null until consumed, then stamped; a used or expired token must never authenticate again). Index on `tokenHash` lookup pattern (however this codebase's existing token models index that — match it).
   - `SiteSession`: `id`, `siteVisitorId` (FK, cascade delete), `projectId` (denormalized for a fast per-project session validity check, mirroring FormSubmission's own denormalization habits if you see any), `tokenHash` (the session cookie's value, hashed the same way), `expiresAt` (30 days from creation), `createdAt`. This is what the actual browser cookie's value maps to after hashing.
   - Do NOT run `prisma db push` or any DB command yourself — write the schema, then tell me in your final report to run `npx prisma db push` (confirmed working convention on this project).

2. **Login request**: `POST /__auth/request` (same-origin only, same host/origin/body-cap checks as everywhere else via lib/site-endpoint.ts's shared helpers — do not duplicate that logic). Body: an `email` field (validate with the existing `STRICT_EMAIL_RE` from lib/site-endpoint.ts). On a valid-looking email: find-or-create the `SiteVisitor` for (projectId, email), create a `SiteLoginToken`, email a magic link `https://<slug>.kodely.site/__auth/verify?token=<raw>` (reuse the site's own base-URL helper the existing code already has, e.g. `siteBase`/similar in site-forms.ts). CRITICAL anti-enumeration requirement: the same-origin HTML reply must say the exact same thing ("If that email has an account here, or can have one, we've sent a sign-in link.") regardless of whether the address is new, existing, mail-configured or not, or rate-limited — never let a response reveal whether an email is already registered. Rate-limit this same two-axis way the confirmation email was just built (per-project AND per-recipient-address, reusing `createBurstLimiter` from lib/site-endpoint.ts) — this endpoint is a stronger phishing/spam-relay vector than the records confirmation email since it's an unauthenticated "send me a login link" trigger, so be at least as strict.

3. **Login verify**: `GET /__auth/verify?token=<raw>` (same-origin). Look up by hashing the raw token and matching `tokenHash`; reject (same generic "that link isn't valid" style reply as the records manage-link, anti-enumeration, using `timingSafeEqual` for the hash comparison like the existing manage-link check does) if not found, already used, or expired. On success: mark the token used (one-time use, enforced — a replay must fail), create a `SiteSession`, set an HTTP-only, Secure, SameSite=Lax cookie (host-scoped, no `Domain` attribute, distinctly named e.g. `kodely_site_session` — never anything resembling the portal's own cookie name) containing the session's raw token (only its hash stored server-side), and redirect (303) to the site's own home page or wherever `_next` (same control-field convention as records) points, defaulting sensibly.

4. **Logout**: `POST /__auth/logout` (same-origin, same CSRF-equivalent origin check as every other POST here) — deletes the matching `SiteSession` row and clears the cookie, redirects back.

5. **Reading the current visitor identity during a GET request**: in app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts's GET handler, read the session cookie (if present), hash it, look up a non-expired `SiteSession` scoped to this project, and resolve the current `SiteVisitor` (or null). Pass this into the existing `renderSiteRecords()` (lib/site-record-render.ts) call.

6. **"My records" read-back**: extend the `data-kodely-records="<kind>"` convention with an additional boolean attribute, `data-kodely-mine`, meaning "only render records created by the CURRENTLY authenticated visitor" instead of all active records of that kind. This requires: (a) `SiteRecord` gets a new nullable `siteVisitorId` column (FK, cascade delete — add to the existing model, don't create a new one), (b) `submitSiteRecord()` in lib/site-records.ts must stamp `siteVisitorId` on create IF (and only if) a valid `SiteSession` cookie was present on that same-origin POST (same session-resolution logic as step 5 — factor it into a small shared helper both the GET route and the POST record-creation path can call, rather than duplicating the cookie/hash/lookup logic twice), (c) `renderSiteRecords()` filters by that visitor id when `data-kodely-mine` is present and a visitor is authenticated, and renders the container's own static empty-state (or a sensible "sign in to see this" fallback if genuinely no visitor is authenticated — do not silently show nothing with no explanation) when `data-kodely-mine` is present but no visitor is currently signed in.

7. **Update/cancel for authenticated visitors**: extend the existing token-based update/cancel path (`POST /__records/<kind>/<id>`) so that if a `SiteRecord` has a `siteVisitorId` AND the request carries a valid session cookie matching that same visitor, the update/cancel is allowed WITHOUT requiring `_token` in the request — a real "you're logged in, just click cancel" flow. The token-based path must keep working exactly as before for records with no linked visitor (anonymous submissions) or for a visitor who has the link but isn't currently logged in.

8. **Teach the builder model**: add a new section to lib/agent.ts, parallel in precision to the Records section, explaining exactly: the `/__auth/request` (email field) → confirmation page → magic-link email → `/__auth/verify` → session cookie lifecycle; the `data-kodely-mine` convention; that this is entirely magic-link (never build a password field, never ask the model to hash or check a password — there is no password path in this system at all); and how a "my account" page combining a sign-in form + `data-kodely-records data-kodely-mine` container is genuinely buildable now.

CONSTRAINTS (non-negotiable):
- No passwords anywhere in this system, ever.
- No CSP relaxation — everything works via cookies + same-origin form navigation, exactly like the records system.
- No sharing of cookies, session tables, or token logic with Kodely's own portal auth (lib/auth.ts) — completely separate, host-scoped cookie.
- Anti-enumeration on both the login-request reply and the verify-failure reply — never reveal whether an email has an account.
- One-time-use, time-limited login tokens, `timingSafeEqual` for hash comparisons (matching how the existing manage-link token check already does this — read that code and mirror it).
- Keep `kind`/`fields` on SiteRecord exactly as generic as before — `siteVisitorId` is just an optional linkage, not a new constraint on what a record can be.
- Do not touch the still-independent token-based manage-link flow's core behavior for anonymous (non-visitor-linked) records — it must keep working unchanged.

STEPS:
1. Read every file listed above in full before writing code.
2. Implement the schema additions.
3. Implement request/verify/logout endpoints, dispatched from app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts alongside the existing `/__forms/`, `/__records/` dispatch.
4. Implement the session-resolution shared helper, wire it into record creation (visitor stamping) and the GET handler (for `data-kodely-mine` rendering).
5. Extend the update/cancel path for session-authenticated owners.
6. Update lib/agent.ts.
7. Run `cd /c/Users/edmem/kodely-prod && npx tsc --noEmit -p .` and `npx eslint app lib components --max-warnings=0` — both must be completely clean before you finish (expected pre-existing-until-migration errors are fine to note, e.g. new Prisma fields not yet in the generated client — call those out explicitly rather than leaving them unexplained).

Report back: the exact new endpoint shapes, the exact cookie name/attributes used, how anti-enumeration is enforced on both the request and verify replies, how the shared session-resolution helper is used in both the GET route and record creation, and the exact command I need to run.

33	// The last three directives do NOT inherit from `default-src` — that is the
34	// whole reason they have to be written out. Without them the "no external
35	// requests" contract had a hole big enough to walk a phishing form through:
36	// `connect-src 'none'` stops fetch/XHR and stops nothing else, so
37	// `<form action="https://attacker.example">` submitted cross-origin and
38	// carried whatever a visitor typed.
39	//
40	//   form-action 'self' — the only POST a generated page may make is to its own
41	//     origin. Everything else — <form action="https://attacker.example">,
42	//     formaction= on a button — is refused by the browser before a byte leaves.
43	//     Contact CTAs of the tel:/mailto:/sms: kind are <a href> and form-action
44	//     does not touch them either way.
45	//
46	//     UNCHANGED BY FORM SUBMISSIONS, and that is the point. Generated sites can
47	//     now have working contact forms (lib/site-forms.ts, POST below), and this
48	//     directive did NOT have to be widened by a single character to allow it,
49	//     because `'self'` is the SITE's origin — https://<slug>.kodely.site — and
50	//     that origin is already us: proxy.ts rewrites every request on it into
51	//     this very route. So a form whose action is `/__forms/<name>` is a
52	//     same-origin POST that lands in the same handler that served the page.
53	//     Pointing the form at kodely.me instead would have been cross-origin and
54	//     would have meant adding an external origin to form-action on every
55	//     customer site on the platform — a real loosening, for nothing.
56	//
57	//     Note what is still refused: a page may POST to its own origin and to
58	//     nowhere else, and only the paths this route answers do anything. The
59	//     phishing shape this directive was added for (a generated page collecting
60	//     what a visitor types and shipping it to an attacker) is exactly as
61	//     impossible as it was before.
62	//
63	//     `connect-src 'none'` is untouched and must stay that way. A form POST is
64	//     a navigation, not a scripted request, so nothing here needs it — which is
65	//     also why the submission endpoint answers with HTML rather than JSON.
66	//   base-uri 'none' — an injected <base href> would silently repoint every
67	//     relative URL on the page, which is a way to smuggle a remote origin back
68	//     in past the directives above.
69	//   object-src 'none' — plugin content has no use on a static generated page,
70	//     and it does not fall back to default-src either.
71	//
72	// MUST STAY IN SYNC with the copy in app/api/preview/[id]/[[...path]]/route.ts,
73	// which serves the same generated markup to the editor's iframe. It is a
74	// separate constant in a separate file on purpose (that route is owner-only
75	// and has its own MIME table); there is no shared module for the two.
76	const SANDBOX_CSP =
77	  "default-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'self'; form-action 'self'; base-uri 'none'; object-src 'none'";

79	/**
80	 * Which stored build file answers a requested URL path.
81	 *
82	 * Generated sites are multi-page (lib/foundation.ts): `vite build` emits a real
83	 * document per page — index.html, about.html, blog/index.html — and visitors
84	 * ask for /about, not /about.html. This is the whole server-side cost of that.
85	 *
86	 * Deliberately NOT the SPA catch-all ("serve index.html for anything unknown").
87	 * That shape is what a client-side router needs, and it turns every typo, every
88	 * dead inbound link and every stale crawl URL into a 200 serving the home page —
89	 * soft 404s, which Google treats as a quality problem on the whole site. Here a
90	 * path resolves only to a file that actually exists under one of two well-known
91	 * spellings, and everything else still 404s exactly as it did before.
92	 *
93	 * Anything carrying an extension resolves to itself and nothing else, which is
94	 * what keeps robots.txt, sitemap.xml and /assets/* on their existing single
95	 * path — no candidate list can shadow them.
96	 */
97	function candidatePaths(filePath: string): string[] {
98	  if (/\.[A-Za-z0-9]+$/.test(filePath)) return [filePath];
99	  const clean = filePath.replace(/\/+$/, "");
100	  if (!clean) return ["index.html"];
101	  // Order matters: about.html wins over about/index.html when a site has both.
102	  return [`${clean}.html`, `${clean}/index.html`];
103	}

105	/**
106	 * The only POST shapes a published site's own origin ever answers:
107	 *
108	 *  - `/__forms/<formName>`, which arrives here as
109	 *    `/api/site/<slug>/__forms/<formName>` via proxy.ts. Everything — host
110	 *    check, published check, caps, abuse control, storage and the owner
111	 *    notification — is in lib/site-forms.ts.
112	 *  - `/__records/<kind>`, the generic storage primitive behind
113	 *    backend-backed site features (bookings, client portals, simple data —
114	 *    see lib/site-records.ts). Same shape, same safety machinery, no
115	 *    product-specific logic here or there.
116	 *  - `/__records/<kind>/<id>`, the update/cancel target for the "manage
117	 *    this" link `/__records/<kind>` handed the submitter — one path segment
118	 *    longer, dispatched separately because it needs a token, not an origin
119	 *    check alone.
120	 *
121	 * Anything that is not one of these exact path shapes is a 404 in the
122	 * handler it's dispatched to, so this does not become a general POST surface
123	 * on the sites domain.
124	 */
125	export async function POST(
126	  req: Request,
127	  { params }: { params: Promise<{ slug: string; path?: string[] }> },
128	) {
129	  const { slug, path } = await params;
130	  const segments = path ?? [];
131	  if (segments[0] === RECORD_PATH_SEGMENT) {
132	    return segments.length === 3
133	      ? submitSiteRecordUpdate(req, slug, segments)
134	      : submitSiteRecord(req, slug, segments);
135	  }
136	  return submitSiteForm(req, slug, segments);
137	}

139	export async function GET(
140	  req: Request,
141	  { params }: { params: Promise<{ slug: string; path?: string[] }> },
142	) {
143	  const { slug, path } = await params;
144	  const filePath = path && path.length > 0 ? path.join("/") : "index.html";
145	
146	  // Generated pages are only ever first-party to the sites domain. proxy.ts
147	  // turns this request away earlier for the same reason, but a route handler
148	  // must not depend on that: the proxy's own matcher can miss paths, and the
149	  // proxy is explicit (see its header comment) that it is never the only gate.
150	  //
151	  // The response is byte-identical to the "no such site" 404 below, so it does
152	  // not confirm that a slug exists to someone probing the wrong host.
153	  if (!siteHostAllowed(req.headers.get("host") ?? "", slug)) {
154	    return new Response("Site not found.", { status: 404 });
155	  }
156	
157	  // `/__records/<kind>/<id>` — the "manage this" link handed out by
158	  // lib/site-records.ts's create reply. Dispatched here, before the file
159	  // lookup below, because it is not a stored file at all; everything about
160	  // it (host check, token check, the invalid-link reply) lives in
161	  // lib/site-records.ts, same division of labour as the POST dispatch above.
162	  if (path && path.length === 3 && path[0] === RECORD_PATH_SEGMENT) {
163	    return viewSiteRecord(req, slug, path);
164	  }
165	
166	  const project = await db.project.findUnique({ where: { slug } });
167	  if (!project || !project.publishedAt) {
168	    return new Response("Site not found.", { status: 404 });
169	  }
170	
171	  const baseUrl = siteBaseUrl(req, slug);
172	  const seoHeaders = {
173	    "Content-Security-Policy": SANDBOX_CSP,
174	    "Cache-Control": "public, max-age=60",
175	  };
176	
177	  // robots.txt and sitemap.xml are generated, not stored — they depend on the
178	  // visitor-facing host (which differs between the branded subdomain and the
179	  // staging path form), so a file baked at build time would be wrong on one of
180	  // them. A site that ships its own copy still wins: we only synthesise these
181	  // when the project has no such file.
182	  if (filePath === "robots.txt" || filePath === "sitemap.xml") {
183	    const own = await db.projectFile.findFirst({
184	      where: { projectId: project.id, path: filePath, published: true, kind: "build" },
185	    });
186	    if (!own) {
187	      if (filePath === "robots.txt") {
188	        return new Response(robotsTxt(baseUrl), {
189	          headers: { ...seoHeaders, "Content-Type": MIME.txt },
190	        });
191	      }
192	      const pages = await db.projectFile.findMany({
193	        where: { projectId: project.id, published: true, kind: "build", path: { endsWith: ".html" } },
194	        select: { path: true },
195	      });
196	      return new Response(
197	        sitemapXml(baseUrl, pages.map((p) => p.path), project.publishedAt ?? undefined),
198	        { headers: { ...seoHeaders, "Content-Type": MIME.xml } },
199	      );
200	    }
201	  }
202	
203	  // One query for both spellings of a page, then the caller's preference order
204	  // decides — /about must not cost two round trips to answer.
205	  const candidates = candidatePaths(filePath);
206	  const matches = await db.projectFile.findMany({
207	    where: { projectId: project.id, path: { in: candidates }, published: true, kind: "build" },
208	  });
209	  const file = candidates.map((c) => matches.find((m) => m.path === c)).find(Boolean);
210	  if (!file) {
211	    return new Response("Not found.", { status: 404 });
212	  }
213	
214	  const ext = file.path.split(".").pop() ?? "";
215	
216	  // Backstop so no site can ship with the foundation's placeholder <title>.
217	  // Only fills gaps — anything the builder wrote itself is preserved.
218	  //
219	  // pageUrl(), not baseUrl: canonical and og:url must name THIS page. Keyed off
220	  // the file that actually answered, so /about and /about.html both canonicalise
221	  // to /about and Google sees one page rather than two competing duplicates.
222	  // Live read-back (Phase 1B): a builder-authored `data-kodely-records="<kind>"`
223	  // container gets its matching SiteRecord rows rendered into it, server-side,
224	  // per request — see lib/site-record-render.ts. Runs BEFORE applySeo() only
225	  // because there is no ordering dependency between the two and this keeps
226	  // "content" and "head metadata" as two separate passes over the string,
227	  // each easy to reason about alone; applySeo() never looks at anything this
228	  // step could have touched (it only touches <head>).
229	  const body =
230	    ext === "html"
231	      ? applySeo(await renderSiteRecords(file.content, project.id), {
232	          projectName: project.name,
233	          baseUrl,
234	          pageUrl: pageUrl(baseUrl, file.path),
235	        })
236	      : file.content;
237	
238	  return new Response(body, {
239	    headers: { ...seoHeaders, "Content-Type": MIME[ext] ?? "application/octet-stream" },
240	  });
241	}

1	// WHICH HOSTS MAY SERVE A CUSTOMER'S GENERATED HTML.
2	//
3	// The site route renders arbitrary attacker-authored markup with
4	// `Content-Type: text/html` and a CSP whose `'self'` resolves to whatever host
5	// the request arrived on. On <slug>.kodely.site that is exactly right: the page
6	// is first-party to its own site and to nothing else. On kodely.me it is a
7	// first-party page on the application's own origin, with a real certificate and
8	// the real domain in the address bar — a phishing surface. Nothing in the route
9	// or the proxy used to look at the Host header at all, so
10	// https://kodely.me/api/site/<any-published-slug>/ served that page to anyone.
11	//
12	// This is an ALLOWLIST, not a block on the app domain. A blocklist would have
13	// to enumerate every name the app answers to (apex, www, the admin host, any
14	// future one) and would fail open the moment one was added.
15	//
16	// The `/api/site/<slug>` path form is NOT the bug and is not removed: staging
17	// depends on it, because there is no wildcard DNS for *.kodely.site off prod, so
18	// staging.kodely.me/api/site/<slug> is the only way to look at a published site
19	// there. lib/site-seo.ts derives canonical and og:url from precisely this
20	// subdomain-vs-path distinction, and both forms below keep producing the URL
21	// they produced before.
22	
23	const SITES_BASE = (process.env.KODELY_SITES_BASE ?? "kodely.site").trim().toLowerCase();
24	
25	// Where the path form stays legitimate. Overridable so a second staging
26	// environment does not need a code change; the default is what deploy.sh
27	// deploys and verifies.
28	const STAGING_HOST = (process.env.KODELY_STAGING_HOST ?? "staging.kodely.me").trim().toLowerCase();
29	
30	/** Host header minus the port, lowercased. Handles bracketed IPv6 literals. */
31	export function bareHost(host: string): string {
32	  const h = host.trim().toLowerCase();
33	  const v6 = h.match(/^\[([^\]]+)\]/);
34	  if (v6) return v6[1];
35	  return h.split(":")[0];
36	}
37	
38	function isLoopback(bare: string): boolean {
39	  return (
40	    bare === "localhost" ||
41	    bare.endsWith(".localhost") ||
42	    bare === "127.0.0.1" ||
43	    bare === "::1"
44	  );
45	}
46	
47	/**
48	 * May this Host serve the published site `slug`?
49	 *
50	 * Three shapes, and nothing else:
51	 *
52	 *  1. `<slug>.kodely.site` — the branded subdomain, which proxy.ts rewrites to
53	 *     this route. Note it must match THIS slug: `a.kodely.site/api/site/b/` is
54	 *     refused. That is not the reported finding, but it is the same mistake one
55	 *     level down — it would let any customer host any other customer's page on
56	 *     their own site's origin, where `'self'` and `frame-ancestors 'self'` both
57	 *     resolve to the victim site's name. The legitimate rewrite always agrees
58	 *     with the subdomain, so nothing real is affected.
59	 *  2. The staging host, on the path form, because staging has no wildcard DNS.
60	 *     Staging is not the application's public identity; a page served there is
61	 *     not a credible impersonation of kodely.me, and reaching it means the
62	 *     victim already accepted a staging URL.
63	 *  3. Loopback, so local development and `next start` testing keep working.
64	 *
65	 * Everything else — kodely.me, www, the admin host, any bare IP, any Host a
66	 * caller invents — is refused.
67	 */
68	export function siteHostAllowed(host: string, slug: string): boolean {
69	  const bare = bareHost(host);
70	  if (!bare) return false;
71	
72	  const wanted = slug.trim().toLowerCase();
73	  if (wanted && bare === `${wanted}.${SITES_BASE}`) return true;
74	  if (bare === STAGING_HOST) return true;
75	  return isLoopback(bare);
76	}

1	/**
2	 * The NAMES of the two auth cookies, and the pure helpers for reading the
3	 * non-sensitive one — deliberately in a module with no imports at all.
4	 *
5	 * It exists because three places that must never disagree about these names
6	 * cannot all import lib/auth.ts:
7	 *
8	 *   - lib/auth.ts itself, which owns writing both cookies;
9	 *   - proxy.ts, which runs on every request and must not drag Prisma (and
10	 *     therefore lib/db.ts, which lib/auth.ts imports) into the proxy bundle;
11	 *   - components/marketing/useSignedIn.ts, which runs in the BROWSER and
12	 *     could not import a server-only module even if it wanted to.
13	 *
14	 * Copying the strings into each would be the same mistake getCurrentSession
15	 * in lib/auth.ts already argues against: a nav that quietly disagrees with
16	 * the real cookie name shows the wrong thing forever and looks like a bug in
17	 * sign-in rather than a typo in a constant.
18	 */
19	
20	/** The real session cookie. httpOnly, opaque token, hashed in the database. */
21	export const SESSION_COOKIE = "kodely_session";
22	
23	/**
24	 * The HINT cookie. Readable by JavaScript, on purpose, and therefore it must
25	 * carry nothing worth stealing: no user id, no email, no name, no role, no
26	 * token, no fragment of one. Its entire vocabulary is the single literal
27	 * "1" below, which means "a session cookie was present when this was
28	 * written" and nothing else. An attacker who reads it, forges it, or hands
29	 * it to someone else gains exactly one thing: a marketing nav that says
30	 * "Portal" and a /dashboard that bounces them to /login, because every
31	 * authenticated surface still goes through getCurrentUser() and the database.
32	 *
33	 * It exists so that a STATICALLY PRERENDERED marketing page — which cannot
34	 * read a cookie on the server, by definition — can still show the right two
35	 * nav links without the whole marketing site being forced dynamic.
36	 */
37	export const AUTH_HINT_COOKIE = "kodely_auth";
38	
39	/** The only value the hint cookie is ever given. Anything else reads false. */
40	export const AUTH_HINT_VALUE = "1";
41	
42	/**
43	 * Matches SESSION_DAYS in lib/auth.ts. It is a ceiling, not a promise: the
44	 * hint is written alongside a real session with the real session's expiry
45	 * wherever that expiry is known, and proxy.ts deletes any hint whose session
46	 * cookie has gone. This constant is only for the backfill path in the proxy,
47	 * which has no database and therefore no way to learn the true expiry.
48	 */
49	export const AUTH_HINT_MAX_AGE_SECONDS = 30 * 24 * 60 * 60;
50	
51	/**
52	 * True when a cookie string contains the hint. Takes the raw string (either
53	 * `document.cookie` in the browser or a Cookie header on the server) rather
54	 * than a parsed jar, so the same function is usable from both and testable
55	 * from neither.
56	 */
57	export function readAuthHint(cookieString: string | null | undefined): boolean {
58	  if (!cookieString) return false;
59	  for (const part of cookieString.split(";")) {
60	    const eq = part.indexOf("=");
61	    if (eq === -1) continue;
62	    if (part.slice(0, eq).trim() !== AUTH_HINT_COOKIE) continue;
63	    return part.slice(eq + 1).trim() === AUTH_HINT_VALUE;
64	  }
65	  return false;
66	}
67	
68	/**
69	 * What proxy.ts should do about the hint, given what the request carried.
70	 *
71	 * Split out as a pure function because the interesting behaviour is a
72	 * two-cookie truth table, and the failure that matters — telling a signed-out
73	 * visitor they are signed in — lives in exactly one of its four rows.
74	 *
75	 *   session  hint   ->  action
76	 *   ------------------------------------------------------------------
77	 *   yes      yes        "none"   the ordinary signed-in request
78	 *   no       no         "none"   the ordinary anonymous request
79	 *   yes      no         "set"    a session that predates this feature
80	 *   no       yes        "clear"  STALE: the session cookie is gone
81	 *
82	 * Only the two disagreement rows touch the response, so neither an anonymous
83	 * visitor nor a settled signed-in one ever gets a Set-Cookie header they did
84	 * not need — which is what keeps this safe to run in front of the
85	 * statically-cached blog pages.
86	 */
87	export function authHintAction(
88	  hasSession: boolean,
89	  hasHint: boolean,
90	): "none" | "set" | "clear" {
91	  if (hasSession === hasHint) return "none";
92	  return hasSession ? "set" : "clear";
93	}

It works the same way contact forms do — a plain HTML form 155 POSTs to the site's own origin, no fetch, no client state — but instead of 156 being emailed to the owner, what you write is stored as structured data you 157 choose the shape of, and you can read it back into the page and let a visitor 158 manage what they submitted, all without a login system. This is genuinely new 159 capability, not a trick: use it whenever the brief calls for something that 160 needs to remember rows of data — a restaurant's reservations, a gym's class 161 roster, a shop's inventory, a CRM's leads, a directory of listings, RSVPs, 162 anything structured. It does not turn a static site into a general app: there 163 is still no server code, no database query YOU write, no accounts, and 164 everything under "Never build something that only pretends to work" above 165 still applies to anything this pattern does not cover (checkout, live search, 166 login). 167 168 There are three moving parts, and a real feature uses at least the first and 169 usually all three: 170 171 **1. Writing a record — \`POST /__records/\`.** You invent \`\`: it 172 is not a fixed template, it is whatever the business actually needs, one kind 173 per distinct "type" of thing being stored (\`reservation\`, \`class-signup\`, 174 \`listing\`, \`lead\` — pick a name that fits the brief). Markup shape, same 175 rigor as the contact form above: 176 - form: method="post", action="/__records/" 177 - the same hidden honeypot input named "_gotcha" (visually off-screen, 178 tabIndex={-1}, autoComplete="off") and the same hidden "_t" timing input 179 set to Date.now() on mount — required, verbatim, exactly as for a contact 180 form; this endpoint is exposed to the same spam. 181 - real fields: whatever the record actually needs, each a labelled, 182 required input where that makes sense. 183 184 Rules, all enforced server-side: 185 - \`\` MUST be lowercase \`[a-z0-9-]\`, starting with a letter or digit, 186 32 characters or fewer — identical rule to a form's \`\`. 187 - Every real field needs a \`name\` matching \`[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_-]{0,63}\`, 12 188 fields maximum per record, each value capped around 5000 characters. 189 \`_\`-prefixed names are reserved for control fields, exactly as in a 190 contact form, and are never stored as data. 191 - \`method="post"\` only, no \`fetch\`, no client-side logic beyond \`required\`. 192 193 What happens after a successful submit: unless you set a hidden "_next" 194 field to redirect the visitor to a page of your own, Kodely shows them an 195 automatic confirmation page with a private, one-time "manage this" link — 196 a long, unguessable URL that lets THAT VISITOR come back later and change 197 or cancel what they submitted.
